study.title: 2 Samuel 21 - Justice, and the mighty men of David
study.overview: This chapter brings together two main blocks. First, hunger is linked to Saul's guilt against the Gibeonites, and reparation involves the surrender of descendants of Saul's house, followed by a reverent burial resulting in the relief of the land. Then the text records several wars against the Philistines, showing that although David is the king, the preservation of Israel depends on God and also on the courage of his servants. The chapter unites justice, allegiance to oaths, compassion for the dead, and the continuity of divine protection over Israel.

outline.title: The famine and consultation of the Lord
outline.explanation: David seeks the cause of the famine, and the LORD reveals that it is bound to the blood shed by Saul against the Gibeonites. David then negotiates with the Gibeonites to seek a reparation that leads to the blessing on the inheritance of the LORD.

outline.title: Repair, mourning and burial
outline.explanation: The Gibeonites refuse silver or gold and ask seven descendants of Saul, but preserve Mephibosheth because of the oath between David and Jonathan. Rispa watches the bodies with painful fidelity; David collects the bones of Saul and Jonathan, joins them to those of the executed and burys them with honor, and then God becomes favorable to the earth.

outline.title: The Last Fights with the Philistines
outline.explanation: The text features different Philistine warriors and their giants. David is almost wounded, but his servants help him; then, other mighty men of Israel defeat the enemies, ending with the remembrance that the giants of Gath fell by the hand of David and his servants.

study.context: Notes indicate that these final chapters of 2 Samuel function as a closing section, organized by themes and not necessarily in chronological order. The chapter contrasts Saul's guilt and David's faithfulness, and also between the threat of the Philistines and the action of God through David and his warriors. The immediate historical setting is the kingdom of David, but the text highlights more theological reading than the exact chronology.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that collective sin and oath break brings real consequences, even when the guilty act occurred before. The correct answer is not simple vengeance, but reparation before God and respect for the covenant made with the Gibeonites. The preservation of Mephibosheth shows that oaths before the LORD continue to force the king's conscience. Rispa embodies faithful and insistent mourning, and the burial of the bones suggests that honoring the dead and repairing injustice are part of the restoration. In the second part, the defeat of the giants shows that Israel's victory depends not only on David's strength, but on the hand of God working through his servants. When David is weak, the text shifts the focus of his ability to divine fidelity.

scholarViews.insight: The picture of conflicts with the Philistines highlights the deeds of David's warriors, and when David appears tired, the focus shifts from his strength to God as the source of Israel's success.
The section on hunger recalls Saul's ancient offense against the Gibeonites and shows that the pending guilt can reach the nation until it is treated before God.
Hunger is presented as unknown in the previous narrative, and the cause pointed out is Saul's violence against the Gibeonites, although this fact had not been recorded before.

questions: What attitudes does the chapter suggest when an ancient injustice continues to produce effects on the present?
Why does David preserve Mephibosheth, even before the need for reparation requested by the Gibeonites?
How does David's fragility in the battle help to show that victory belongs to the LORD and not just the king?
study.practice: Examine whether there is any moral or spiritual obligation left without reparation in your life: a broken promise, an unrecognized injustice or a word that needs to be corrected. Also practice a faith that does not ignore the pain of others, such as that of Rispa, and remember that God can use ordinary servants to protect and sustain his work. When reading this chapter, transform reflection into concrete actions of truth, reconciliation and fidelity.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text records David's response and the final result, but does not fully detail the mode of justice involved in the surrender of Saul's descendants. Notes also indicate uncertainty about the exact date of events and some textual details, such as identifying certain names at 21:8 and 21:19. Thus, some chronological and genealogical relationships remain discussed in interpretive sources.
